utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone after this long weekend. Mr. Ierace. Let me just first ask the Registrar to call the case, because I had forgotten that. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, you may recall that last Friday, the Prosecution sought leave to change the order of witnesses. The next witness will be retired squadron leader Carl Harding, and he will be taken by Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed the change of order in your absence, Ms. Pilipovic, as you might have heard meanwhile. Mr. Usher, could you please bring the witness into the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next witness is in a wheelchair, and I should make clear that the circumstances in which he came to be in a wheelchair have nothing to do with what happened in Sarajevo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's good to know. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to begin with. Thank you for giving me the floor. Here I wish to mention that the Defence had only extremely limited time, not to say no time at all, to prepare for the cross-examination of this witness for the reasons that you know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Harding, as I understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, before giving testimony in this courtroom -- first of all, welcome in this courtroom -- the rules require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text of this solemn declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher. And since I do understand that you speak English, I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding. Mr. Waespi, you may examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Harding.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Waespi:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please introduce yourself to the Court with your full name.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: My name is Carl Daniel Edwin Harding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: 14th September, 1964.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I'm married?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, may I immediately ask you both just to pause for a while so that the translators are able first to translate the question, and then to translate the answer because if you continue speaking in the same language on a continuous basis, then they will not be able to follow it. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me briefly go through your military career. Is it correct that you served with the Royal Air Force regiment for 16 years, and you retired in March 2000?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Royal Air Force regiment is the branch of the RAF that has responsibility for ground defence?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's correct, therefore, that your training is akin to that of an infantry office, even though you served in the RAF?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go to your service in Sarajevo. What time did you arrive in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I arrived in Sarajevo late July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: In January 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the exact date when you left?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Approximately the 23rd of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in Sarajevo, in what capacity were you there?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I was there as an unarmed military observer, which was given the name of "UNMO."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your initial assignment as an UNMO, and where was your initial posting?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: My assignment as an UNMO was to observe and to report all military activity from either side. My first position was known as PAPA 1, which was a gun position high on a hill on the northern side of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say -- first of all, perhaps UNMO, what does UNMO stand for?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: UNMO is United Nations military observer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you just mentioned also "PAPA." What does "PAPA" stand for?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: PAPA is from the phonetic alphabet and it stood for Presidency which identified that I was within the city. If I was outside of the city, all signs would be LIMA, and that stood for Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And LIMA observers would observe which weapons of which warring faction?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: LIMAs would observe on the Bosnian Serb side, and PAPA would be within the city for the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us how many PAPA locations were there at your time, and perhaps you can refer to a map in telling the Judges where these positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I would like the usher to give the map numbered Prosecution Exhibit 3644, a fresh one, to this witness. I understand that later it will be identified as H, but perhaps the Registrar can be more specific. Mr. Harding, if you can briefly look at your screen because there you can see what part the Judges...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was just trying to make sure I can see them all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just take your time. As soon as you have had the chance to orientate yourself, we will ask you to identify the old PAPA positions you were aware of at the time you arrived, and please take us through starting with Number 1. And after you have started, perhaps you can be provided with a blue pen so you can mark with a circle and add the number to it, which PAPA location you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: PAPA 1 was on the hill below the television transmitter area. PAPA 2 was lower down the same hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps one second to say for the record, you are using I think a black pen, and you are making triangulars. But it doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Actually, I think a blue pen is used, and it should be a blue pen because blue is the colour for the Prosecution. It's rather dark blue, and the triangulars is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's blue pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: PAPA 3 was located in a small office block next to the Lion Cemetery. PAPA 4 was the old olympic stadium. PAPA 5 overlooked the railway lines and barracks at Rajlovac. There was two positions. The southern one was the observation post. The northern one was for administration and where you would sleep. Observed from this one and slept and administration at that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you can mark the northern one with an A, 5A, and the southern one with a B.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: [Marks]. And finally...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we please have it on the ELMO before you mark it, yes, so we see your hand on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's difficult to see on a photocopy. And the headquarters of the PAPA side UNMOs was in a building adjacent to the Presidency in the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, was there also a time when a PAPA Number 6 was established?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, the positions I've shown were the positions when I first arrived in Sarajevo. After reconsideration, some of the positions were moved so as to provide better locations from which to observe. Can I mark the new locations on the map? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: With a circle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: To start, PAPA 1 was withdrawn completely as the weapons moved. PAPA 2 was moved along the side of the hill and was fairly close to where it was originally, but the house was much higher and had a much better view. It was just higher up the hill. PAPA 3, which overlooked the Lion Cemetery, was withdrawn. PAPA 5, the two locations for PAPA 5, were both withdrawn. New PAPA 5 was put in place which directly overlooked the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you perhaps at this point tell us what the PTT building was.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The PTT building was the headquarters for UN operations at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to show us on the map where that building was?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Approximately this location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you can also draw a circle and add a "P" to it.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: PTT building, in this area. It's difficult to tell on this map where the main UN headquarters were. There's also the location for our field hospital run by the French.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this change of P5, for instance, did come into effect?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: PAPA 5 was moved about September of 1992, I can't remember the exact date. The new observation post was put in place, known as PAPA 6. PAPA 6 was high on the hill directly south of Bistrik barracks, which is where the Egyptian battalion was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was PAPA 6 established?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Without referring to my notes, it's about late September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence has one objection. Could the map be zoomed in to enable us to precisely locate it and what is it where it says PAPA 6. We simply cannot see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could it please be zoomed in a bit more so that the Defence is better able to...

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: PAPA 6 was high on the hill just below the treeline. It had a purpose-built observation post, and the administration area was in a house right next door to it and on the treeline. It was high on the hill. It looked over all of the old city and west to the hills on the other side of the valley -- I'm sorry, east to the hills on the other side of the valley. The aim of these -- this redeployment was PAPA 6 could see the eastern end of the city, the new PAPA 2 could see the centre of the city, and PAPA 5 could see the west end of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harding in general--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, what was the reason for the establishment of a PAPA observation point? Let's take PAPA 1 where you were at initially. Why was there an observation post?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: At PAPA 1, which is high on the hill just below the television transmitter, there were four 105-millimetre Howitzers, small field guns. With those guns, there were 50 personnel, and they lived in a house next to their weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it correct to say that PAPA locations were placed where there was weaponry, military equipment from the AH side?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: That's correct. PAPA 1 had the field guns. PAPA 2, which was below, had some other mechanised pieces of equipment. PAPA 3 had some other APCs, armoured personnel carry yes, sir, and PAPA 4, there were some mortars and vehicles to move these. PAPA 5 was the only true observation post when I first arrived in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if the location of a PAPA was moved, what was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The reason to redeploy all of the PAPA call signs was because they were not doing proper observation duty of the city, and the equipment that they were with was very static in that it didn't work or they did not have any ammunition for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For instance, the APCs you have mentioned at PAPA 3, did they ever move?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me take you back to PAPA position 1. These men you described, I think you mentioned the figure of 50, were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: There was 50 men. The occasional one would have a camouflage jacket, and one or two would have camouflage trousers. But the majority of those 50 men were in normal civilian clothing without small arms, without helmets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the four artillery pieces at PAPA Number 1. Were these pieces active?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: When I arrived, the guns had not been active for some time. They had had ammunition. The empty boxes were there, as were the empty cases. But you could tell by the area around each gun and the way that it was dug into the ground, there must have been firing when the ground was wet and fairly sodden because you could see boot marks and footprints. But now the whole area was completely dry and everything had shrunk down to lock the weapons in place. They hadn't moved for at least a week and a half when I first arrived, which would have been end of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the static PAPA observation posts which you had identified number by number, were also patrols made?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: When I first arrived, the patrols were normally on administrative duties. However, there was one location that had T-55 tanks, and that was checked every day by a patrol. Later on, when the observation posts were moved, there was a much greater patrol in order to monitor the armoured vehicles that once had PAPA observers next to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned tanks, T-55 tanks, I believe you said. Can you tell us the locations of those tanks?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: There were two T-55 tanks, and they were in a tunnel where vehicles would go through. There were two tunnels, one of which wasn't finished because there was no road connecting it. The other one was used all the time. On the northern end of that tunnel, the tanks were just inside and just parked up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these tanks, to your knowledge, were they guarded?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: No, there was no guard on them, and we were free to climb on them, have a good look around. We had record of their serial numbers and identifying features. But they were just static with nobody there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times were they checked, these tanks but also other ABiH weaponry?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: At a minimum, they would have been checked twice a day, once in the morning and once late in the afternoon. But as the vehicles were moving around, as the UN vehicles were moving around, they were on a very popular route and therefore were driven past numerous times each day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding. Now, you said you were initially stationed at PAPA 1. Was there a time you moved to PAPA 5?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, I stayed at PAPA 1 for four or five days until I'd finished digging defensive bunker. I then moved on to PAPA 5, which overlooked Rajlovac barracks at the western end of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were there at PAPA 5, can you tell us of a specific incident which you recall?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: In the initial PAPA 5, the -- I'll show you on the map. As I said at the start, PAPA 5 was split into two locations. This location was for the sleeping and administration --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. This location, you just pointed at 5 --

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, at location 5A, the northern location was in a house, administration. The location 5B was the observation post that was manned at night. There was one occasion where I was manning location 5B, which was in a house that was only half built, the building next door to me was engaged by heavy weapons such as 12.7 millimetre heavy machine-gun or 20 millimetre anti-aircraft gun. All these buildings are made of very soft building, and we just had to stand our ground. There was also occasion when I was at 5 alpha, the front line is very close to it on the northern side, to the east of it, and to the west of it, so there was an occasion where there was a large gun battle in the area, firing down the street in front of our house, as well as numerous mortars landing approximately 75 metres from our house. This was the second position that I manned, and I was there for approximately three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you act as an UNMO in the observation post PAPA 1 and PAPA 5?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I was an UNMO until late September when I became part of the PAPA headquarters staff initially with the post of logistics officer. In that post, I was responsible for resupply of all of the PAPA UNMO positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time that you also became operations officer?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes. Started at logistics, and at that time there was an operations officer as well as a subsector commander. So there were three people on the headquarters. I became logistics officer. The operations officer was moved out of the sector, was not replaced, and I became the operations officer and second in command for the PAPA UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you perform this job as an operations officer?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I was doing both those jobs until the 23rd of November when I became the subsector commander on the PAPA side. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your superior as a subsector commander?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: My superior, when I became the subsector commander, was Lieutenant Colonel Richard Mole. He was posted out from the sector and was replaced by Lieutenant Colonel cut -- Cutler.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding. Now, as a subsector commander, what were your duties and what were you in command of?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Subsector commander is in command of all the PAPA UNMOs, that's all the observation posts, patrols, responsible for resupply, collation of information and tasking PAPA side UNMOs for utility repair duties as required and any other duties required within the sector. I was responsible for those PAPA side UNMOs in all respects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many UNMOs were under your command?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The number would vary, but on average the -- between 20 and 25. All officers, captains and above, three of them were lieutenant colonels, and my rank was a major.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one last question before we move on to a specific incident: Having seen these UNMO posts, especially PAPA 1 and PAPA 5 but also others which you have [indiscernible], did you form a view about the professionalism of the ABiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: When we come into direct contact with these soldiers, at PAPA 1, there was 50, or at PAPA 4 which is the location under the stadium, the majority were -- had minimum training. An example would be PAPA 1 gun position, one of the men had been a costume designer and maker for the television studio. Three and a half months later, he is now manning artillery pieces, and that's just one example of the civilian professions. You could tell by the way they acted, the way they were dressed, that the majority of them were basically civilians, just minimum training, enough to see them past the piece of equipment that they were supposed to man, but nothing more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding. Let's now talk about some specific incidents. First of all, was the Lion Cemetery in your area of observation?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: When I first arrived, PAPA 3 was in the bottom of an office block and directly overlooked the Lion Cemetery as it had a clear view to the north and to the stadium up here. Even when this position was withdrawn, it was then part of our patrol route. We would stop at PAPA 3, check the armoured vehicles next to the office block, get passed the Lion Cemetery and on to PAPA 4 at the old olympic stadium. So this cemetery and this position were checked twice a day by the patrol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you may have answered that already, but was there a time when PAPA 3 had moved?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes. It had been a static position. It was decided that the men -- the UNMOs there could be better used in observation posts and patrols. So we withdrew completely from PAPA 3, and we moved all of our stores and all of our defences, which were mainly sandbags.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Lion Cemetery, while you were there, did it increase in size?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: When I first arrived, the graves were being dug by a mechanical digger, and extra graves were dug between graves which were obviously prewar. By the time I left, the cemetery had overflowed. Directly opposite was an all-weather football pitch, and graves were dug into that football pitch and on to the grass next to it. And they were usually dug five to ten at a time while the people were there. By the time I left, that football pitch was half covered with graves. So yes, the cemetery did overflow after all of the area had been used and was infill between graves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this Lion Cemetery, did funerals take place?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They took place all the time. Sometimes three or four at a time. And then there were formal occasions, each one of them, as time would allow, because there was so many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these funerals ever subject of attacks?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Funerals were a fairly common thing to be attacked, and so it wasn't unusual. You didn't stay around -- near the cemetery to watch a funeral because you risked -- there was an increased risk of an attack. So funerals could be observed from PAPA 4, which was to the north and at the olympic stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say they were attacked, who attacked those funerals? Where did the shots originate from?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Attacks on the funeral had come from the north and slightly northeast. I'm indicating on the map north, PAPA 4, around to the east. And they come from the Bosnian Serb forces. That is the location of the front line in this area. An example, north of PAPA 4 was the front line. You went inside the stadium in the centre, then there was a risk of sniper fire, to give an example of how close the front line was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the sniper fire would originate from which part of the -- which side of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: From the Bosnian Serb side. So this area here, north of 4, around to here, PAPA 3. And the attacks on the cemetery were from that location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, could you please, for the sake of the record, indicate where the witness is pointing at, which might not be quite clear if we do not describe it. Or ask the witness to mark the locations he indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That's what I was going to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can tell us again where the sniping fire originated from.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The witness just drew four interrupted lines north of observation post 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps you can add an S, letter S, to the right end of that line.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Marks -- the dotted line marked with an S is the approximate location of the front line at that time. So the Lion Cemetery can be observed from the front line, front line just north of the stadium. And so the stadium was subject to sniper fire from some of the buildings here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And "the buildings here," can you perhaps draw a little circle and a P indicating that these are the buildings you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The front line was fairly fluid here because there are buildings. It's difficult to draw exactly where it was as it did move. But it was from the buildings to the north could put fire on to the stadium, and also the drive leading into the stadium from its east side, all over around this Number 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the record, the Lion Cemetery, can you make a cross and add L to it.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: PAPA 3 and the small cross are side by side, because PAPA 3 was at the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harding. Now, can you describe to the Trial Chamber one of such attacks, and first of all, my first question would be, did you witness the attack yourself?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: There was an attack on the 23rd of October, 1992. The attack was observed by Major Nikolai Roumiantsev. Excuse my pronunciation. Roumiantsev. He was from the Russian army. He was doing a patrol and had stopped at PAPA 4. He was due to return driving down the road from the stadium here at PAPA 4, you can see the stadium mark there. Straight down the road, but he could not return because a funeral in the Lion Cemetery was under attack by mortars. He stayed and watched the duration and reported -- would have reported it over the radio to the PAPA headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding. And you just indicated that this Russian major, he travelled between PAPA 4 towards on that street you said, towards PAPA 3, and then he had to stop.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes. He was due to drive past PAPA 3, which is passed the Lion Cemetery, but to do so was too dangerous. He had to wait and watch until the mortar fire stopped, and then he could drive back to the headquarters. Then on the 24th, I was informed there had been damage to the old PAPA 3 building, and I went to see the state of the damage in case we needed to reoccupy it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding. Did the Russian major report any casualties to you?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: It transpired that as a result of that attack, some of the people at the funeral tried to take cover in the old PAPA 3. It used to have sandbagged walls which you could then get behind for safety. Unfortunately, when we moved, we took everything with us. Some civilians tried to take cover where they thought there was sandbags, but a mortar round struck the door that they were trying to go through. A 21-year-old woman was killed and some men were injured. When I went to look at the old building at PAPA 3, the remains of the woman were still on the floor as they were the pieces that could not easily be picked up by the medicine medics to clear it out. There was sufficient remains left to attract wild birds who were eating the remains when I arrived. These remains were in the rubble next to the door and blood could be seen by the door where she had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you go to attend the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I went to that location the next day, as soon as I could go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you recall the exact time the incident took place the day before as reported by your subordinate, Major Roumiantsev?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the exact time. But it was in broad daylight. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. couldn't say whether it was morning or afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that it was mortar fire who had caused that incident. Can you be more specific, for instance, about the calibre?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: It seemed that it was mortar fire because at that time there were a lot of trees in the Lion Cemetery. And -- and it was also on a hill. The trajectory of the weapon must have been fairly steep to clear the trees and to hit the door -- it was on ground floor. And so the way that it had come in, must have been a mortar, an 81 or 82-millimetre mortar. I didn't find the tail of the mortar round which can be found sometimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your own observations and from what you were told by your subordinates, did you form any conclusion as to where this shelling originated from?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: To attack the funeral, someone must have been watching to see that people were in the cemetery, and someone must have been controlling the fire to bring it to bear on the cemetery. The observation posts must have been to the north of PAPA 3, to the area of the front line indicated by the dots on the map. This area here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It is difficult to tell exactly where you're pointing at.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The forward observation officer must have been to the north of the Lion Cemetery on the higher ground indicated by the dotted line on the map, and he would then be able to see the cemetery and control the fire. Therefore, it must have come from the north because that was the only way that the cemetery could be observed. Therefore, the observer must have been from the Bosnian Serb army because they held the high ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day when you went to that location, did you take pictures?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I took pictures of where the round struck the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, if the usher could please distribute Prosecution Exhibit P3662. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When have they been communicated to the Defence, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any observations from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So we cannot accept them at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could assist, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just have a glance through the photos, and the Defence has got them by now so that I at least can have a global idea of what the Court is to decide upon. utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I will do so, Your Honours. Just one point of clarification: These six photographs don't go beyond the witness statement. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, that's what was in the back of my mind. If these photographs would need a thorough study and if it would be anything else than just an illustration to what the witness testifies, then of course we might consider the matter in a different way. Please proceed. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will remember, Your Honour, that a few weeks ago I asked that our work during the week be organised differently. utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI

utterances.text: Then they should have been told to the Defence at least on Friday -- not on Friday. The last day last week was Thursday that we were sitting. I'm sorry for the mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the investigator who had taken the statement didn't take them with him. And this witness, as you know, was originally planned to be a witness under Rule 92 bis. So when he was called, we realised that he should, being a viva voce witness, take everything with him which was attached to the statement. That's the reason for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. For the time being, I would say -- Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence must also tell you that at that time, the witness presented these photographs for inspection and said he was willing to hand them over if they were required so that when his statement was made, these photographs were described and they were offered to the investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber does understand by now that whether the photographs were in the hands of the Prosecutor or not, they at least were available on the request to the Prosecution a long time ago. I invite the Defence to look at the photographs during the break, and as it was indicated by the Prosecution, that they would just be an illustration of what the testimony is, to consider whether not objecting to them would be better in order to find the truth, a better understanding, since confusion hardly ever assists in preparing decisions. But once you've given your point of view after the break, Ms. Pilipovic, the Court will then decide on whether they are admitted in evidence or not. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, just one last point of clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In the witness statement which has been correctly described by my colleague from the Defence, these six pictures are identified and described what they portray and, of course, as we said before, they were handed over later. But let me, of course, continue with the next subject before the break. I would like to add, though, at this juncture that together with these photographs, also three reports were given to us by the witness also on Thursday. And as we go along in the examination-in-chief, I will also refer to these three documents, three reports. And they have the same, I guess, fate, to a certain extent as the photographs, although when the investigator had visited the witness in May of last year, he could not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. find those reports. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: Please respond, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. As I said before, and as we had communicated to the Defence in writing on Friday, we do intend to tender these three reports, and I had just mentioned a couple of minutes ago that these reports were mentioned in the witness statement, as were the photographs, but we could not retrieve them because the witness, who signed, who drafted these reports, could not find them and we were also not able to find them in our offices. So yes, they were not disclosed because we didn't have them. Once we had them, that was Thursday night, we had disclosed them. As you will see, Your Honours, these reports are quite short, four and five pages. The battle assessment damages from two hospitals, and there is a two-page report. Again, everything is mentioned quite in detail by the witness in his witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, of course you may respond. I do not intend to spend the next 12 minutes -- we still have until the break to repeat what is quite clear to everyone by now, that is, that these reports could not be found at that very moment. I don't know how much effort has been made since then to retrieve them. But at least they have not been communicated to the Defence until Thursday evening or Friday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is another point I wish to raise, Your Honour. It was said that these are short reports. I would like to know whether they were translated into B/C/S in view of the fact that they are short so that the accused can also study them during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, unfortunately, Your Honours, we did not have time, I have to say obviously, to translate these official UN reports into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll give a decision after the break. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, as part of your duties, did you carry out battle damage assessment on hospitals?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What triggered this reporting?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: On the 7th of December, 1992, I was ordered by the senior management officer to send the patrol to both hospitals to see the conditions and to find out what had happened on an attack on the Kosevo hospital. I sent my second in command, who at that time was Captain MacDonald from the Canadian army. He went to Kosevo hospital and was informed the attack the previous day had killed one nurse, injured another nurse, and four males. He wrote a report I gave to the SMO, and later, on the 30th and 31st of December, I conducted a battle damage assessment of the Kosevo hospital and the citizens hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding. You said you made these reports to the SMO. Can you tell us who the SMO is?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: SMO at that time was Lieutenant Colonel Cutler from New Zealand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honours, I would now ask leave that these two reports can be shown to the witness so he can identify his signature and also tell the findings he made. I can also add in terms of translations that I recall the pretrial judge, Judge Rodrigues that passages of these reports can be read out and the interpreters in the booth can translate it into a language the accused understands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's better that we have a break a bit earlier than usual so that we can consider the matter that is in front of us. We will adjourn until 11.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It took us as you may have noticed a few minutes more than we expected to come to decisions as far as the admission into evidence is concerned of photographs and some reports, military reports. The problem this Chamber is faced with is the following: On the one hand, the more material we have, not just in testimony but also in visualizing what is part of the testimony, the better we might be able to understand exactly what has happened. So in our search for the truth, there might certainly be helpful these photographs and these documents. On the other hand, if photographs and documents are presented as evidence, the fairness of the trial would require that the Defence gets enough time to prepare for the cross-examination of the witness who has testified about these photographs and about these documents. Especially as far as the photographs are concerned, it is the understanding of this Chamber that they were available already quite some time ago, and no proper action is taken to get them into the hands of the Prosecution itself. As far as the documents are concerned, we do understand that they could not be found at that very moment, and I can leave aside that at this moment whether more action could have been taken to retrieve them in an earlier stage. What does it mean as far as our decision is concerned? Let me start with the photographs. The photographs, as we understand, are merely an illustration of what the testimony of the witness will be about. Therefore, it would assist the Chamber to better understand to have a look at them. At the same time, Defence counsel might look at photographs in a totally different way as the Prosecution does. If we would decide not to admit these photographs in evidence, the Chamber misses an illustration but at the same time the Defence would presumably miss an opportunity to challenge what is on those photographs and by these means, also to challenge the testimony of the witness. So before taking a final decision on the photographs, I'd like to invite the Defence to give their point of view, and especially in view of the illustrative character of the photographs, and a possibly lost opportunity to challenge the content of the photograph and also the -- perhaps the testimony of the witness. I'll tell you in advance that if you continue to object, that this Chamber will decide that they will not be admitted into evidence. So just say that your objection stands, and it will not be admitted into evidence. Nevertheless, I'd like to have your view on it. And let me add just one thing: If you would lift your objection, you will have an opportunity at a later stage if necessary to cross-examine the witness on the photographs itself. That would mean even if this could be done only not immediately, subsequent to the examination-in-chief, the Chamber will allow you even if it's necessary to recall the witness in order to be cross-examined on these photographs if they are admitted into evidence. But again, if your objection stands, we will not admit them in evidence. So it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before I state the Defence's position, have I understood you properly if I say we are merely talking about photographs; we are not talking about the reports?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then about the photographs, because we examined other photographs the other day which enabled us to establish a different ballistic trajectory than the other one, we will accept these photographs, likewise, although we had no time to prepare for them. But we accept them now, which doesn't mean that we shall also accept the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the objection has been lifted, the photos if tendered into evidence will be admitted. And if necessary, you'll have an opportunity to cross-examine the witness after you have been able to properly prepare for the cross-examination. Let me come to the documents: The documents might not be merely illustrative although we do not know for sure. At least the Defence should have an opportunity to look at the context of the documents and this Chamber is also of the view that on these particular documents, the accused himself should have an opportunity to study them thoroughly. That means that the documents will not be admitted in evidence if tendered at this moment since there's no translation, since the Defence has had no opportunity to study them, especially the accused has had no opportunity to study them. This does not mean that they might never be admitted into evidence, and they are -- the same is valid as in respect of the photographs. The existence of these documents has been discussed here. The witness will testify, as far as I must assume at this moment, on incidents on which -- to which these documents do relate. Since the documents have not been disclosed, the Defence is not in a position to properly prepare for the cross-examination. Therefore, whether you tender the documents in evidence or not, the Defence will have anyhow the right at a later stage to have the witness recalled in order to finish the cross-examination and then in full knowledge of what the documents the witness was referring to, or even if he has not referred to, but the incidents the witness referred to, that at least the Defence has full information about what is available on these incidents to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Prosecution. We would allow -- just for the sake of finding the truth, we would allow if the witness would not have all details still in his mind, we would allow him to read one or two lines as requested during questioning. I must be quite clear to the Defence that while the documents cannot be admitted into no evidence at this very moment but even if they will not be put in evidence at a later stage on request of the Defence, you'll always have an opportunity to finalise the cross-examination, having full knowledge of what the documents are about. Is that clear to both parties, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is more or less half clear, Mr. President. I do not know whether this witness will be available for a long time here, and I do not know if one day will suffice because I have just explained it to the Registrar, even though this problem is not there, that we simply have no assistance. That is, as of this evening, I won't be able to work alone, and we shall again have the chronological --

utterances.text: The problem is such that even if it would be necessary to ask the witness to come back to the Hague at a later stage. Of course, if it's not necessary, let's try to prevent it. But if necessary, it has to be done. Yes? Does this clarify the part you did not fully understand yet? It's clear to the Prosecution as well? Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I merely wanted to say that I'm taking note that at a later stage we can even imagine that a few days later it will happen. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or a few weeks, yes, of course. That's a practical matter. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think, yes, the witness could be recalled at a later stage if his schedule will permit that. And as you know, he sort of jumped out of order appearing right now, so I'm sure that could be accommodated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I just first make one remark to Mr. Harding. Mr. Harding, when you might have got a feeling that we are masters of your time; we are not. When I'm talking about a possible recall of you as a witness, of course a suitable time both for the court, for the parties, has to be found. But I just want to avoid you thinking that we are masters of your life. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the second point is, are we allowed to put these documents, these two documents, the two assessments, which were drafted by the witness, just purely mark them for identification as they are, and put it to the witness so he can at least identify that these were the documents he had drafted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we -- if you would ask him, let's say, to read of it a few lines or whatever, if you would allow him to use it in order to refresh his memory, I think it's good that they have been at least marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI

utterances.text: So, please, Mr. Harding, let's go back to these hospital damage assessments which we talked about at length now in a procedural way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First let's turn to the first report, the exhibit or the document, rather, Number 3661, that's the document titled "Battle damage assessment, citizens hospital, operations effects," and the date is 2nd of January, 1993. Now, Mr. Harding, do you know another name for the citizens hospital?

utterances.text: Yes, it also referred to as the "French hospital."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, perhaps as suggested by Judge Orie, the presiding judge, you could perhaps read the introductory portion of this document so we can get a feel to this point, and perhaps we can even narrow it down to the second part of the introductory comment where you start with "I ensured...

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: All of this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, it is our understanding that you would examine the witness on the general parts of it without using the document, and use the document only if it comes to some specific details. I don't know whether you'd regard, especially the second part of the introduction in such a detail. If yes, please proceed. If no, please examine the witness in the ordinary way. It will not be tendered into evidence as you know; it will just be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. One minute, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Harding, these two reports, did you draft those two reports?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these two reports, I mentioned the first one, the battle damage assessment, citizens hospital, operational effects of 2nd of January, 1993, that's a document marked as Prosecution Exhibit 3661. And the second report is a document now called Prosecution Exhibit Number 3660, and it's entitled "Battle damage assessment of Kosevo hospital, operational effects." Now, without referring to these documents, can you tell what the role was you saw in yourself when you visited these two hospitals?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I was in Sarajevo as a military observer, and I decided that I would conduct these battle damage assessments with a view to identifying military actions that had been taken against the two buildings and the effect that that military action had on the operational capabilities of the hospitals. I was not there as part of a UNHCR or as an NGO operation. It was purely from a military point of view as I was a military observer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In conducting these two reports, you said before the break that you went to see the two hospitals. For how long did you stay there, did you talk to people, did you visit locations?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: When I went to both hospitals, I was met by the directors of both hospitals and the senior members of his staff. I was then given a tour of the whole hospital complex. It would have taken half a day to cover the whole area, Kosevo being spread out more than the citizens hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding. Now, in your recollection, was -- and now turning to the citizens hospital or also French hospital as you had called it -- was the hospital ever marked?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, that hospital had been marked. It had a large white flag with a large red cross, and the flag was hanging from the hospital from the top floor at the centre on the south-facing part of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just finish with one question. You may in fact have answered that already. After you have done the reports, you have filed it or you have given it to your superiors or to whom?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: As soon as I had finished the reports, which is one or two days after the inspection, I gave them to the SMO, Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler. And then he gave them direct to General Morrillon's staff, and I understand that action was taken as a result of the reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what kind of action General Morrillon took after this report was received?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: He arranged and ordered for a large generator to be placed on the grounds of Kosevo hospital in order to provide electricity to the heating system and also for critical elements within the hospital. It was a very large generator, and it was white with "UN" written on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, I would now move on to a different subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like Mr. Harding to talk about the use of tanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned the tanks you saw on the ABiH side, and we can come back to that later. Talking about tanks from the Bosnian Serb side, let me take you to the 24th of September, 1992. Do you recall where were you at that date?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, I was in -- I was at the PAPA 5 observation post which was in the new position number one where it was when I first arrived. The PAPA 5 I referred to was on the hill directly north of the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding. Can you describe to us what you saw when you were at PAPA 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on page 37, line 6, there is a problem with the interpretation. It seems to me that something has not been interpreted quite correctly. Urgent, an extraordinary situation, that's the word that was used, an emergency, and I would like to draw your attention to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not exactly understand what you -- you say there's a problem on page 37, line 6. What is missing in the -- is it the French translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am speaking of the French transcript. I am telling you what I heard, and this is not what is in the French transcript. So I wish to mention it to avoid any misunderstandings later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it vital for our understanding at this moment or can we leave it to those who work on the transcript this evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm drawing attention to it now because I feel it is important. If we are speaking of an emergency situation, we can draw the conclusion that this was caused by shelling and it's important to say so. The English transcript does not mention an emergency situation anyway in the context of the testimony about generators that can be used in extraordinary situations, in emergency situations. The Defence raises such issues only when it considers them to be important. If you feel it is not important, we apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we know exactly what the French transcript reads so that I can compare it with the English or?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not actually have the French transcript in front of me, but I know what I heard from the French booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Special attention will be paid to page 37, line 6, and we will be able to compare it, if there's any reason to come back to it once they have been corrected, as you know that happens overnight, please draw my attention to it and assist me again, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, can you describe to the Trial Chamber what you saw on 24th of September, 1992 while you were at PAPA 5?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I was at PAPA 5, which is on the hill north of PT, looking south down the road which was known as the airport road, which led directly to the airport. This road --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you perhaps move the map a little bit so Your Honours can see where the airport is.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Zoom out some more. I was here at PAPA 5 looking south, and I could see directly down this road which leads to the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you, perhaps, use your marker and draw the line where the road is located to which you are referring.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Witness just drew a line, I understand left -- a couple of centimetres left of the road to which you are referring to. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please indicate it by an R, saying it is the road you just talked about.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I was in PAPA 5. I could see straight down the road marked as an R. I watched five T-55 tanks come down the road and head north. They were in a line astern, one behind the other. The barrels of the tanks were pointing towards the east and to the west. They had no infantry support. They drove down the road firing at the buildings left and right, some as close as 50 metres. After a while, they turned around and went back down the road, that being down heading south continuing down the road which goes towards Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: As they were firing, the empty cases from the armament were discharged from the tank, in other words, thrown out on to the road and on to the sides of the roads. When the tanks had gone, you drive down the road which is also the main road to get to the airport, there was in excess of 100 empty shell cases, the shell cases being at least half a metre long. That meant that each tank would have fired around about 20 rounds. And those empty cases were there for some weeks after, and they would being run over and just pushed off the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, could you see any military targets besides the road or were these military targets to which the tanks fired at, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: From my position, at PAPA 5, I could see no obvious targets for the tanks. There was no infantry support for those tanks, if an operation was underway. I've driven down that road many times. It was very much a No-Man's Land in that the buildings had received substantial damage, and there was little gain in trying to move around them because they gave little cover. So to answer your question, no, I could see no reason for those tanks to do what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the tanks fire again when they turned back and went the other way around?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: As they were moving backwards and forwards on the road, they were just firing, so when they decided to withdraw, they just withdrew up the road and ceased firing at that stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did this firing last? I think you used the term "for quite some time."

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I would need to -- the exact time would be in my diary. But it wasn't a quick drive up the road and fire. They slowly came up the road, started to fire, occasionally moving, and then they just withdrew. I could see no reason for them to be -- to do that. Because when they had gone, there was no change in any situation in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that the closest building was 50 metres away from the tanks. Do you recall how far the furthest building was away from the tanks which was hit by the tanks?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: From what I could see from that position, all the targets were fairly close because it's very flat where the tanks were. And on the map you can see there are buildings either side of the road. Although they were damaged, it meant that the line of sight from the tank could not be far because the buildings were in the way. And the tank only fires at a direct weapon; in other words, it has to see the target in order to hit it as opposed to artillery that does not need to see the target because it can fire overhead. But the tanks was a straight line, so from 50 metres, maybe out to 300, 400. But not very far because of the buildings all around there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described five tanks doing this action. Was that a controlled, commanded, coordinated action, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Well, to have five tanks moving must have taken some orders. A troop of tanks, I did not feel it was one or two individuals' own actions because each vehicle will have a crew, and also there was a danger that one of those -- one or more of those tanks could get damaged, as along that road there was already one T-55 that had been taken out and that was damaged and was seen regularly on television as it was at an angle of 30 to 40 degrees off the side of the road. So I think if those tanks were to go down there, on the word of just one person, a loss of a tank would have been quite significant as they are a key asset. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me move to a different subject, a different weapon system. Mr. Harding, have you seen the use of multilaunch rocket system in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you, in fact, tell the difference between this system and artillery or mortar? I mean, can you tell the difference? What would you put into this position to say that? Do you have experience in that?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, I have experience of all three of those weapon systems. The main one that you mentioned, artillery, it became common to hear artillery flying overhead. And you had a constant but very faint noise as the round went over. It was only when that noise changed that you knew it was in descent and may come close to you. But when it was in transit, it was a very faint noise. I could compare that to a multilaunch rocket system because -- it's not going to do. There was an occasion where I took my second in command to see the old PAPA 1 location here. At that time, we continued passed it, around to where my marker is, directly west of the old PAPA 1. On this position, on that day, we had been observing shelling, and the shells were landing to the west of PAPA 1. It was particularly memorable because as we stood here, there was one artillery round that we would refer to as a "drop short" in that it came into its descent before its intended target. And it landed very close to myself and the 2IC, my second in command. On that day, as we were walking back, there was a multilaunch rocket system that was fired over our heads, and you could hear several projectiles, the flight of them was slightly staggered. They had a high-pitch whine as they went overhead. They then came overhead, and we looked to the east, towards our headquarters here as marked previously in the map as HQ. We then saw the multiple impacts of the multilaunch rocket system land east of our headquarters, and we estimated at 3 to 400 metres. From where we were to where they landed, we could draw a straight line as indicated by the mark, my marker, like that. So we were at the old PAPA 1. They landed east of our headquarters. Therefore, they were fired from the northwest, which goes over to Stup.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date this incident happened? Perhaps the month would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: That occurred on the 8th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said they landed a couple of metres beside the headquarters of the PAPA. Can you mark it on your map, please.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes. From the distance that we were observing, I would say it is 3 to 400 metres east of the headquarters. How would you like that marked?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps, again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have by now a range that if something is marked, if two points are there and it says that it's 3 or 400 metres east, that we are able to measure that on a map. I mean, it's -- unless it's not really east, then of course it might be different. Perhaps would you first ask the witness that. If it's really east, then we can just count 3, 400 metres east from the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is east of the PAPA headquarters, because from our position we could see it was the other side of PAPA headquarters and only estimate 3, 400 metres because from our range, it was quite difficult to observe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to discern any military target they were firing at on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: At that occasion and at that time, areas east of our headquarters were just civilians, although there were military personnel around with no known military concentration and there was no known military operation going on at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Harding, in the Sarajevo military theatre, who used this rocket artillery, multilaunch rocket system?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: It came from the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges how this system works and what sort of target it would be used against.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Multilaunch rocket system fires numerous munitions that are slightly staggered -- at a slightly staggered interval and are used for an area target. In other words, they are not for pinpoint one trench; they are for an area that can be a hundred metres square or something like that. And there are numerous rocket-propelled pieces of artillery, and the number of them can vary according to the individual weapon system, as they do range from small ones which can be towed by a vehicle such as a Land Rover, the larger ones are mounted on the backs of trucks. They are an area weapon, not a point weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, Mr. Harding, an "area weapon," is that a suitable weapon in an area -- to fire into an area where the possibility of the presence of civilians is?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: No, not in an urban area such as that, and you cannot guarantee that they will land exactly where you want them to land. So no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was it used by the Bosnian Serb army? Was it used according to the way you think it should be used or was it used in a different way? For instance, the sequence of shots.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Well, it would normally be used for an area target which is known enemy or troop concentrations, not endanger your own forces. But in this case, I would say there was no known military forces, although the weapon was fired correctly as in operationally, it fired all of its munitions at a staggered interval, but into an area where it was predominantly civilians. And it was not in support of a military action. In other words, if there was an advance, then to clear the ground ahead of the advance, you could see the multilaunch rocket system. But there was no advance. It was no support of any military action. It was merely firing weapons into an urban area occupied by civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, 8th of December, 1992, how many rockets were fired?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I could say it would be not less than nine. But we couldn't count them individually, because we had just recently been subjected to shelling ourselves when we had the drop short. But I would say not less than nine, which also aided the identification of a multilaunch rocket system rather than artillery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware whether single shots were being fired using this weapon system?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Single shots from that weapon system may well be able to occur, but I haven't heard single shots from a multilaunch rocket system. That would be the job of artillery. You'd fire them all together, as that's the way that the system works.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges the sound of this weapon system.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier on, we knew the sound of artillery, both in its transit and its descent. Mortar rounds usually do not give any warning because of their steep descent, whereas these weapons had a high-pitch scream, I suppose, would be the best description of it, or a howl, as they went overhead. They made a very distinctive noise, so they were very easy to identify as not being artillery and being a weapon of special effect rather than the normal artillery that went over. So it was a scream or a howl. And as there was not less than nine, those were easier to identify them as they all went over that maybe one second or one and a half second intervals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your experience of being there and having seen, observing, yourself, you talked about the civilians, do you know what the effect of this weapon system was on the civilians in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I did not follow up the observation of the rocket system, and I did not go and inspect the damage. But from what we observed from the old PAPA 1, the damage to buildings, the roofs, the tiles, and other such like damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this system a significant weapon? Is it more important than others in the arsenal of an army?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Normally, I would consider this weapon to be significant because it uses a specific type of ammunition. There may be a lot of artillery ammunition or tank ammunition that these weapons are not common and they do use a special ammunition. So I would consider this weapon to be considered as an important fire support weapon because of logistics needed to support it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The rounds themselves, are they expensive?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Monetarily, I would consider them probably more expensive, although I have not had cause to actually work out how much in money terms that they would cost. So I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe the last question: Could you form, from your experiences, an opinion about the psychological effect this weapon had on the civilians? The weapon, and also the way it was used.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The psychological effect on the civilians was usually hit by the use of single rounds of artillery and mortar. This weapon was not used that often, but it did not give any warning for those that were the target, whereas single rounds from artillery, a mortar, which was common, had a greater effect on the psychology of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to another system, weapon system, anti-aircraft artillery. Are you familiar with anti-aircraft artillery, and can you describe its use and effect to us.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Anti-aircraft artillery can range in calibre from 12.7 millimetres, often referred to as a "heavy machine-gun" through to 20 millimetres and increased to 56 millimetres. The idea of anti-aircraft Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. artillery would be to put ammunition in the air ahead of an aircraft so that the aircraft flies into it, rather than trying to chase an aircraft. The ammunition would have an explosive head, so if it would hit the aircraft it would cause damage to the aircraft as well as penetrating into the aircraft.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have described these calibres. Did the -- as far as you're aware, did the Bosnian Serb army possess this type of artillery, the weapons and the calibres you had mentioned?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, they did. And they could often be heard because the larger the calibre, the slower the rate of fire. And throughout my term, they had high rates of fire, from the smaller calibres, 12.7, to a slow rate of fire which is steady dug from the 40 or 56- millimetre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I take it from what you have just said that you have experienced anti-aircraft artillery yourself while you were in Sarajevo?
