utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, I have experience of a 20 millimetre anti-aircraft artillery when I first arrived in PAPA 5. That was used on the building next door. And I've seen it used on the other buildings, and it could be identified because the rounds, once they exploded and had penetrated a wall, had lost their kinetic energy, you could fire them into the building and you could pick them up. On the rounds, they had the calibre, 20 millimetres, and it also had Cyrillic letters on it, which I didn't know what they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, can you perhaps take us to one incident where you saw the use of anti-aircraft artillery yourself?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: There was one occasion where I was at the observation post at PAPA 6 as I indicated on the map with a number 6. South of the location were the Bosnian Serb army. At that one occasion, I was standing at PAPA 6 when a weapon, anti-aircraft artillery of 12.7 millimetres opened fire over my head and straight down into the city. You could clearly see where the rounds were landing because they have explosive heads, and you could see the white flash. Also, when a weapon like that fires, it has a zone where it lands, which you could call the beaten zone. All the rounds will be spread out. They are not one behind the other. On that occasion, we saw the rounds landing on the roof tops of the city. The weapon then traversed towards the east, firing as it did, as it traversed you could see all around hitting the roofs with white flashes. It then traversed back, so it's firing directly over our heads again, and also the rounds moved backwards and forwards as the weapon was traversed or elevated up and down. Once you'd returned, once you'd swept down the city and back again, then it stopped firing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please mark on the map the areas which was covered by this weapon, and also a line to indicate that traversing, if you may.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: It is difficult to try and assess it with this map. They would have fired towards where I have put the letter "I" for impact, here, traverse to the right, traverse to the left, and then stopped. So it would have been an area -- this is an estimation as it's difficult to show.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for the record, the witness just moved his pointing stick between the outer two ends, the two 0s of the symbol he just drew below the letter I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Harding, did you just use a black or a blue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Blue. These rows to represent the beaten zone where the ammunition was landing, landing in here across.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where was the source of fire in relation to the positions of the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The fire came from directly south of PAPA 6. It's a very steep hill. Somewhere in the area of the arrow that I've drawn. It was very difficult to see because we are on the treeline here, and you can see from the contours on the map, this is very steep. And he was up here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, for the record, the witness just drew an arrow pointing upwards on the map, north I guess, about a hand south of number 6. And are these -- is this area controlled by the Bosnian Serb army where the source of fire originated from?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from your observation point, number 6, did you observe any military target the weapon was engaged to?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: No. There was no military activity at PAPA 6. The ground south of PAPA 6 is so steep, we would have noticed if there's any military activity there. And there was definitely no military activity within the city centre, which is where the rounds and the ammunition landed. It was not prompted; it was not in support of any military action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my last question on this point: You have described the beaten zone of the anti-aircraft artillery. Given that, in Sarajevo, is it suitable for the use in an area like what we have at hand?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I would say no, because the longer the range, the larger the beaten zone. In other words, the longer the range, the more spread out the ammunition will get. This weapon was working at its maximum range, and so totally unsuitable for a military action. But there was no military action in which to support, so it just fired for no reason at all, which makes it all the more memorable because we were looking for something. But it was just -- nothing there. Started for no reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The gunner, in your experience, did he have to use a mechanical traverse device to do what you have described?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The traverse towards the east and then the west appeared to be fairly smooth, and so either the weapon was mounted on some form of platform, because if it wasn't, the recoil of it would mean the rounds would be much further spread than they actually were. And because they were fairly close, we could follow it as it went up the city and back again. It would suggest to me it was on some form of platform with a traversing wheels and traversing mechanism. So yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain that to us laymen what such a mechanism would look like.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The weapon would be mounted in a cradle, and the traverse mechanism would be by turning handles, and that handle would make it traverse left and right. There would be another handle to make the weapon, the barrel go up and go down. In other words, fire into the city at left and right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I think I must intervene because this witness is describing things which he did not see. One would say he is relying on the hearsay, and he turns almost into an expert. And on the top of it, he's making assumptions. I'm sorry I intervened, but I think that now the line has been crossed which the Defence cannot accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think Your Honours it's not hearsay because he's recounting what he has seen or what his impressions were. And second, he is a trained military officer and he can certainly make inferences from what he saw in the field. I also think he has answered the question already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving the decision, may I remind you that we are in a bit of odd system as far as law of evidence is concerned. Since there's no jury here, it will not always be possible to prevent a question from being put to the witness, and sometimes as in this case it has already been answered. So if you are objecting, we also consider this an objection against the use of this information for our considerations. It's known in all systems that there is always a type of a grey area where experience, especially if it's specialist experience, touches upon whether where we really get into the area where only an expert could answer any questions. This Chamber is of the opinion that, first of all, it's no hearsay because he didn't give any source of another person telling the witness what he has testified. Apart from that, that he gave a possible explanation for the way he saw the pattern of the effect of this firing at the city, and the Chamber thinks that this is still within the area where an experienced military man can draw some inferences. But we come close to the field where expertise would have been needed. Please proceed. My decision was that the objection was denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much -- can you give us an estimate of how much ammunition was spent by this gunner or this weapon at this occasion you have just told us?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: It would be very difficult for me to specify a number of rounds that were used, but I have experience of firing, deploying, and controlling automatic weapons up to 12.7 millimetres, firing them myself as well as getting my troops to fire them. And I would have estimated that it would be between 100 and 150 rounds if the weapon was at 12.7 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You already gave sort of an indication of how large or how small, whatever you prefer, the area was, which was covered by the gun. Can you give us an estimate, perhaps, comparing it to -- in metres or to whatever you feel comfortable with?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The beaten zone from top to bottom or north to south as marked on here would have been about 200 metres, two football pitch lengths, and then that area moved to the east and then back to the west. So the furthest would be -- the distance between the shortest and the furthest Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would have been about 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harding. Have you seen this weapon being fired at other occasions than what you just told us?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: There have been numerous other occasions where I had seen heavy weapons such as this firing. They are very distinctive. They have a tracer burn so you can see the rounds in flight, and they have explosive heads so you know that it's a heavy weapon, rather than a smaller machine-gun. And I saw it on numerous times and normally just against buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can go into and maybe even finish another subject before the break. Did you become aware at some point that the ABiH was firing with a mortar from the Kosevo hospital?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: It was reported that the Kosevo hospital had been attacked. I then found out from Colonel Cutler, I think it was, that a staff sergeant had been refueling the generator that had been positioned at Kosevo hospital. Whilst he was there, he saw mortars being fired from within the confines of the hospital. And if the hospital was attacked, it would have been as a direct result of the mortars within the hospital grounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date this incident had happened?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: It was in to January 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say mortars were at the Kosevo hospital, do you know the numbers or the number of these mortars?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: As a result of that, I went to the Kosevo hospital. I looked at the area that the staff sergeant would have been able to see, but I could see no sign of any mortar activity, because they make a very distinctive mark on the ground where their base plate digs in. And if it's on tarmac, it would slide and be dangerous, so it has to be on safe ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What conclusions did you draw from this observation?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: If there was offensive action taken as a direct result of those mortars, it can be referred to as counterbattery fire. However, when I went to the hospital, there was fresh damage as it was only a week or two after I conducted a battle damage assessment. And had the hospital been damaged by a 76 millimetre anti-tank rounds or armour-piercing rounds, and some of these rounds were presented to me, these rounds had hit the building very high up. So even if they had been fired whilst the mortar was firing, they would have been completely ineffective. Six or seven rounds had hit the hospital, and obviously they had been fired by a weapon aimed at the hospital rather than at any mortars that may or may not have been there. So the hospital had been attacked, and it was not a suitable weapon to use as counterbattery fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I read the transcript of what you just said, one sentence starts, it's the second -- third sentence. "And had the hospital been damaged by a 76 millimetre anti-tank rounds or armour-piercing rounds, and some of these rounds were presented to me, these rounds had hit the building very high up." Can you just clarify? Perhaps it's a misstatement. What you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: By high up, I mean that if it was counterbattery fire, it would be aimed at something on the ground, but it obviously wasn't because it was on the first or second storey of the building. So if it had been fired at the same time as the mortars were firing, there was no way at all that it would ever have hit the mortars because it was just fired at the building. The building was the target, not any mortars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you checked the area around the Kosevo Hospital and tried to find the location of the mortar. And you mentioned these markings, the plate marks. So did you observe or did you not observe any such marks?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I found no marks on the ground to suggest that a mortar had been firing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if a mortar was fired, apparently the evidence is if that mortar was fired, what kind of mortar use would that have been?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The staff sergeant didn't specify a calibre, but if it was going to be noticed it was coming from the hospital, I'd expect it to be 81 or 82 millimetre mortar. But I didn't see any base plate marks, and therefore it must have been mounted on something different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps a last subject, a brief one before the break, if the break is taking place at 1.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear overhead the sound of a mortar while the projectile is travelling through the air?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Happened on one occasion. I was at PAPA 1, which is on the hill just below the television transmitter and has been previously described on the map the triangle numbered number 1. South of me, down the hill, ABiH fired some mortars, and they were targeted to the north. As they travelled up on their trajectory, they flew past me, and we could hear them outbound, where normally, you would not hear that. It was only because they were firing up and over the hill, that we could hear them. That was the only time I heard mortars outbound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see mortars employed by the ABiH mounted on trucks?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: No. I never saw any, and I never had any reported to me by any of the observation posts or the UNMOs on patrol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you specifically asked to watch for these kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, we were, because it had been reported they were in operation, but none of us had ever seen them. And so we were told to keep a watch for them to prove or deny all the accusations that were being made at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if that's a convenient time to you, we will adjourn now until 2.30 in the same courtroom. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.57 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just as an introductory comment, the fourth document which was brought to your attention given to the Defence on Friday was proposed Exhibit Number P3659. That's this two-page after incident report of 31st October, 1992. Again, this document was brought with the witness on Thursday, and with your permission, when we go into that incident, I will at the end show it to him, whether he recognises the document, and I will suggest respectfully that this document shares the same fate as the other two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as I indicated before, perhaps later on when all the rights of the Defence are observed properly, then of course whatever these documents can be may be tendered into evidence. But at this very moment since not yet, but marked for identification, fine. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Harding. Were you present in Sarajevo for the Serb Orthodox New Year's Eve?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: No. I don't know the exact date of it, but I certainly remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately which month, which year?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Early January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you certainly remember it. Why?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The sheer amount of fire that occurred to commemorate or to recognise the new year it seemed that every weapon around the city opened up at the same time of all calibres. I was at the PAPA HQ, and we could see -- looking out the windows, we could see tracer all over the sky. My observation post then reported on the radio that there was a lot of activity, and you could hear in the background on their radio messages the amount of fire that was actually happening as they were calling it in. But there was so much that you couldn't indicate exactly where it was going because it was going everywhere at the same time. And it lasted for a considerable time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be more precise in terms of "considerable time"?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Well, you might expect it just to go on for 30 seconds or something, just to commemorate the actual time. But it must have gone on for at least five to eight minutes of automatic fire of all calibres, and so I would say that that's a considerable time, bearing in mind the amount of ammunition that would be expended during that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By automatic weapon by all kinds, can you name a few of the weapons you thought were part of that?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Well, it would start from small calibre, 7.65, rifles right through the automatic series, 12.7, and there were some heavy weapons firing in the background. So I would say probably about 40 millimeters, I suppose. The anti-aircraft weapons, they had a constant discharge of ammunition, steady note going off. And also the amount of tracer that was flying around, you could clearly see it, so it was from the larger calibre, the 12.7s or the 20 millimeters, that sort of size.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when exactly this fire was starting?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: For the new year. It would have been at -- it was midnight. Because it caught me by surprise. When we asked what was going on, that was when we were informed that that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how much of this fire which you just described was in fact Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. hitting the city?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: From my observation posts, they were saying that it was going -- a lot of it was into the air, but also by default it has got to come down. And some of it was into the city. So I would say 50, 60 per cent was going down and the rest was going up into the air to illuminate. So a considerable amount of ammunition was going into the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by city, which parts of the city are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: From that, I would say from PAPA HQ and to the east, to the area known as Stari Grad. Although there was fire up to the western end, up towards PTT and Nedzarici, and [indiscernible]. There wasn't as much as down in the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are saying that 50 to 60 per cent of the projectiles or the -- whatever -- fire was directed into the city?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, by 50 to 60 per cent directed down from the hillside downwards as opposed to up, up on to the hills, into the air, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me move to another incident. That's the 31st of October, 1992. Can you tell us where you were at that time.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: On the 31st of October, 1992, I was in the PAPA headquarters, in the building adjacent to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what happened that day.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I was on radio watch in the headquarters, which just means that I'm manning the radio, making notes of all the reports. At 1000 hours exactly, artillery started to land on the city. One artillery round landed just outside our office. A few minutes later, a woman came into our office and was shouting and waving her arms around. At that time, I didn't have an interpreter, so I stood up, I picked up my rucksack which is full of medical supplies. She then started to indicate to me to go with her. I went downstairs, and I was presented with a number of casualties that had just been hit by the artillery round just outside the office. There was three of them at that time. I looked over the three of them, and I was joined by an Argentinian major who had been with me, and we both started to give first aid to those casualties. As we were administering to those three, another two were brought in. I had a quick look at those and dealt with one of them, which was a fairly simple shrapnel wound. I then moved on to a fairly elderly man. He had shrapnel wounds in his legs, in his stomach, and he was rapidly going into shock. I administered first aid to his wounds, but then I was informed that there was only one or two ambulances in the city, and that they would not be coming to my location, and decided that it was going to be a considerable time before I could get this casualty to the hospital because of the amount of ammunition that was landing on the city, it was a significant barrage. A policeman then volunteered to drive a car, so we took this elderly man on a stretcher and placed him in the back of a police car. To help the stretcher, I got in the back of the car and carried the end of it in so I was against the driver's seat and the passenger seat. When I got out, everybody else had disappeared, so I had to get back into the car. I held on to the casualty, on to the stretcher, and I was leaning out the back of the Volkswagen Golf to stop the door from coming down and crunching on to his legs. We then drove at speed through the city to the Kosevo Hospital where he was taken by the medical staff. Whilst I was there, some press people took some photographs. I then got back into the Volkswagen Golf drove back through the artillery bars. You could clearly see all the dust and debris. You could hear the rounds falling all around. We drove back through that, back to the headquarters where I resumed my radio watch. Because UN personnel had assisted casualties and the press had taken a photograph, I wrote a report of the incident and gave it to at that time it was Colonel Mole so that if anything was said that the UN were helping transport casualties, he knew why it happened and he would then be able to answer the questions at the time, rather than have to find out if regulations had been broken. So although my personal medical stores had been used, no UN vehicles had been used, it was just to make sure he knew what had gone on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding. Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, can you tell us on a map where the location was where you attended these casualties, please.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: These casualties were presented to me in the PAPA headquarters, which is in the building adjacent to the Presidency building on its eastern side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These casualties, Mr. Harding, were these military people or civilian people?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: They were all civilian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see any military target around there which you thought was engaged by the barrages that you had told us about?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: From the round that caused those casualties and from the other rounds that I observed enroute to the hospital, they were so spread out that they were not in one particular location. And so I could not say a specific military target, because they were all over the city. I could see them, and I can hear them, and we drove through the dust from one that got off enroute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they were all over the city," what do you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: "They" being artillery rounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you form an opinion about the source of these rounds you described, the source of fire?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Observation posts were reporting seeing the impacts in the city by the sheer amount of fire in the city -- landing in the city. It could only have come from outside the city, that being the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that the bombardment started at 10.00. Did this timing tell you something?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it did. It started exactly at 1000 hours and stopped exactly at 1600 hours. That was a timed, concerted effort to bombard the city with no specific military objective that could be identified either by myself or by the observers in any of the PAPA positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, have you seen a similar concentration of fire in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, I have observed a similar concentration, and I just need to re-adjust the map so you can see. They need to see this area. If you can see on the map, I'm pointing to the position marked Number 5, which was PAPA 5. It was overlooking the PT. From this position, I could observe across the plain to this area here, which is a small village called Otes. From PAPA 5, I could clearly see Otes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you perhaps indicate with a "T" the broader area, perhaps a circle around it and "T" inside.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The area I refer to has got a blue square around it with the letters "OT" inside. That area is called Otes. I was in the observation post at PAPA 5, and on the 2nd of December, 1992, we observed a concentrated barrage of artillery into the square indicated on the map. That started on the 2nd of December and finished on the 7th, 8th of December. The concentration of artillery and mortars, that continued for a day. There was then an assault with infantry and armoured vehicles supported by tanks, and they gradually worked their way through the buildings until the Serbian army had command of the area of Otes. It was an all-arms attack, that meaning heavy weapons were used to support the armour and the armour was used to support the infantry. It was a very, very intensive use of artillery to the extent that the observers in PAPA 5 could not see or could not count the amount of ammunition landing in that square because there was so much landing at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are saying, from what you observed, that Otes was a proper military attack using artillery and support infantry

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: It was a proper military attack, as you said. Artillery first and then we could see the armoured vehicles and then the infantry, and you could hear the small arms as they worked their way through and took their that area of the ground. It was a controlled attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going back to the incident of the 31st of October, 1992, compared with Otes, how would you describe this attack?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Well, Otes was a proper military attack, and we would have said those former orders to instigate the attack, there was command and control at various levels to achieve the objective which was in such a concentrated area. On the 31st of October, there was no concentration of fire. It was random from what I could see, and from what my observers could see, although it started at the exact time of 1000 and it finished at 1600, there was no obvious objective to be seen by myself or the observation posts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did the timing, what you just referred to, the direction of fire and the range of calibres involved, tell you anything as to the degree of planning involved and the levels -- the command levels which would have been involved?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Do you refer to Otes or the 31st of October?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the 31st of October.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Well, on the 31st of October, all the weapons started to fire exactly the same time, 1000 hours. And there was an obvious ceasefire at 1600 hours. The weapons were from various locations around the city. They must have been by the amount of ammunition that was landing. So there was a certain amount of command and control and orders given for them to start firing at the same time. But the targets that they were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. given were not obvious to us, as the rounds were so spread out as opposed to Otes when all the rounds fell within the square I marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to conclude this part, and to clarify, from which direction or directions was the fire coming on the 31st of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I couldn't really answer that question because we were unable to see the weapons firing, because they were beyond visual range. I couldn't say from which direction as we were just subjected to the ammunition or incoming shelling. But it was from numerous locations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would love to go back to these pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I just ask you, Mr. Waespi, you indicated three hours for this witness. Could you give us an estimate on how much time you'd still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honours. I think ten minutes, quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether you still have the pictures or whether they were taken away. If the potential exhibit, the six pictures, P3662, could be handed to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed, Mr. Waespi, where we used to receive colour copies, I don't know if the colour is of no importance, we'll try to manage. But...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours, for this observation. Because we had to do it in a rush over the weekend and not all the UN services work, especially since a holiday was involved, we will certainly provide you with a colour photograph. And yes, I think it's important that you see the original colours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, if you could take us through picture by picture starting with Number 1, which is the second row, the one in the middle. And you just explain what these pictures display.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Right. The picture now being shown is picture number 1. Where my pointer is, this is the road which leads up to the stadium. This is the turn you would take to get to PAPA 3. This is the Lion Cemetery, which was adjacent to PAPA 3, just here. The thing of note is that all the fencing is down and has been knocked down, and you can see all the new graveyard, grave marked by the new wooden posts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the location of PAPA 3 would be where?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Just out of view around to the right. This goes to a little car park where I'm pointing to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The witness is now pointing to go the lower right corner.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Your vehicle would drive up here to the right and stop, just a very small car park.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, picture number 2, the one immediately to the left.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Picture number 2 I'm showing now is looking directly at the door, that was the main entrance, to where the UNMO stayed. In this area is where the sandbags would normally have been, and just inside is where the UNMOs were accommodated. Behind --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Harding, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The witness mentioned the sandbags and he pointed to the part just where the three, four stairs start if I'm --

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: That's correct. The sandbags were along the top of the stairs and down the side. It would then form some protection for the UNMOs that lived just inside this door. They would go up the stairs and it was on the right-hand side that was their accommodation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You want to add something?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: This is a general shot of where the mortar hit the building, and we had a look, you'll see from other shots, that where my pointer is now --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness points into the middle of the door.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: -- the centre of the door. The remains are still there, and from the crater and the shrapnel -- the damage you'll see in a moment -- where my pointer is now dead centre to those doors is where the mortar round landed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can move on to picture number 3.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Picture number 3 I'm showing now is a close-up of the door. See where the mortar round would have hit, the approximate centre of the door. You see the shrapnel damage on the wall, and it was in this area and over just slightly out of the picture is where the remains of the woman were. In a colour picture you can see there's blood down here and the blood carried on outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And for the record, the witness pointed to the floor of that picture, the lower fifth more to the right of the picture at hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us in relation to this entry of the UNMO PAPA Number 3, how far away were the APCs?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The APCs -- it would be better if we looked at another view of the building. If I return to picture number 2 that we've already seen, the APCs were to the left of this shot and behind the wall to that out of sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the distance in metres?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: It is difficult to estimate it, but in a straight line, if we were to draw it, it would be 80 to 100 metres away around the side and at the back of this building completely out of view. And there was no indication that there was anything there. This building was clearly marked with a UN flag whilst we were there. But apart from that, there was nothing. Access to the vehicles, to the APCs is not via this entrance. They went around the back. And when there were people going to and from them, they were not seen from this side of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harding. Let's move on to picture number 4, please.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Picture number 4, again, is a straight-on view of the door where the round landed. And to the bottom right of the door is where the remains of the woman were, and there was some more mortar to the right. But this shows the damage that was caused by that round.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last two pictures, first number 5.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Number 5 shows the new graves that had been dug. To the right of the graves, you'll see a line of trees --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We were specifically talking about photographs, so could it be more precise. We do not know what time frame we're talking about for each of these photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As far as my recollection goes, the witness has testified that this was on -- I think the day after the impact. But if this is not correct, and as far as I understood, all the pictures were taken the same day. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took these photographs, and they were taken on the 24th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could describe picture number 5, please, continue if there is anything else.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Picture number 5, the new graves that have been dug, to the right, top right corner, you can see a line of trees. That line of trees indicates the road that goes down towards the stadium. On the other side of that road is the Lion Cemetery. These graves are overflow graves from the Lion Cemetery, and you're looking north to take this picture. PAPA 3 is to the right, slightly out of view, and on the other side of the road. This shows the overflow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, picture number 6.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Picture number 6, to the right and the bottom corner can be seen graves that have been dug ready to receive the dead. And on the left-hand side, you can see the start of the all-weather football pitch, and you can see the graves that have already been dug into that all-weather football pitch, and there are ones waiting for the dead and also some marked with wooden grave markers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us in relation to picture 6 into which direction we are looking?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Just double-check on the map. We're looking north as the photo is taken, and the door that we saw that was damaged is also facing north.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding. I would like to ask you a few questions just in clarification of what you have said. You testified earlier this morning about the tunnels, and you said that there were two tunnels. You mentioned that the tanks were in the northern end of one of the tunnels. First of all, can you tell us on the map, indicate please, where these tunnels were.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark it with your blue pen again. Perhaps just two lines for both strings of a -- of the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And that means obviously that these tunnels are moving parallel?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the northern end would be which one?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I see the orientation, it's better to describe it as the western end. The tunnel I refer to is the western end of the southern tunnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you indicate by a cross where you saw the tanks. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I put a cross just by the entrance so the southern tunnel on the western side just inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this the tunnel which was used by the traffic which was open?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, that tunnel has got a road either side. The northern tunnel on the eastern side, there is no road leading to it. It needs a bridge and there isn't one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have also testified this morning that you said prior to you arriving to PAPA 1, there was no firing from PAPA 1, that these artillery positions were not active. While you were there, in Sarajevo, indeed on PAPA 1, was there any firing from those positions?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified this morning and said that there was increased risk of attack, and you explained that around the Lion Cemetery, and you went on to say, and I quote: "You didn't stand around near the cemetery." What do you mean by "increased risk?"

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: By increased risk, I mean that because there was a concentration of people, they were more likely to be shelled or attacked. So you did not stand around when there was a group of people at the cemetery. If there was one or two, perhaps digging graves, it wasn't so bad. But if there was a funeral going on, you don't stand too close to the funeral because there was increased risk, because those people can be seen from positions to the north of the Lion Cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that, and I quote again: "It was a common thing, these attacks." Can you elaborate more what do you mean by a "common thing." Was it a daily occurrence, was it more often, less often?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The difficulty I have is because it happened a lot, it became normal, and because it was considered normal, we didn't make a report on it because it was something that happened. It is very difficult for me to say how many funerals were attacked. It was normal for them to be attacked, although it may seem strange in this courtroom, at the time it was normal. And so we never stood around waiting, watching these funerals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were there between the beginning of August until mid-January. In terms of occurrences of attacks on funerals, was there more attacks before mid-September or afterwards or couldn't you tell?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: With a certainty I can say that the attacks became more common because the trees started to lose their leaves. Eventually all the trees were cut down which then made that area to be in plain view of positions to the north, and so it would be seen that a funeral was taking place and so that it would be attacked. When I first arrived, the trees all had their leaves and you couldn't really see the cemetery from a distance. But as time progressed, the attacks would have increased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that it became normal, these attacks, and because it was considered normal, we didn't make a report on it because it was something that happened." Apart from attacks on funerals, do you recall other "normal things" which you wouldn't report?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: By not reporting, we would report that the artillery rounds or whatever ammunition had landed there. So we reported as a military action, but not record it as an attack on a funeral, if you see what the difference is. Another normal thing was for a single round of artillery or mortar to land at any time and virtually anywhere within the city. This was normal, but it meant every time you went outside, you ran the risk of being caught by these single rounds that were landing. And so these single rounds became normal, and although they would have been reported as seen, it was significant risk to go outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about this single shot you just mentioned. Is there any military sense in firing a single artillery or mortar shot?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Well, there are certain, if you could call them, benefits or objectives from firing a single shot. By doing so, you would achieve maximum surprise. By achieving maximum surprise, you can create the maximum amount of casualties. You also increase the psychological effects on the civilians of the city by doing this because they would always be wary of going outside. From a military point of view, it's minimum effort, because it's only one round, and it's minimum expenditure of ammunition, so you can conserve stocks. So there are five reasons that you could fire one of those rounds. But it was into a civilian area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Against military targets, and perhaps I misunderstood you, against military targets, is there any military objective in using just one round of an artillery piece?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The artillery is usually used in support of a military action, to clear the ground ahead of your own forces or to subdue enemy activity. But normally, you would not fire just one round. The only military time you would maybe fire one round would be to -- it's called fire in, to check fire, before anything was to happen. But that would be on to a specific target. These single rounds were just falling all around the city, and you can't say a specific time because it was completely random. And so there was no military objective for these because they were not on the military targets. They were not on the front lines. They were well away from the front lines. They were inside the -- inside the city, in the main streets, into the market or wherever. It was in the city but no specific location. So from a military point of view, we would say no, because it's not conventional warfare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your -- the Russian major, Roumiantsev, that he reported about this attack on the funeral. Can you clarify again what his position was vis-a-vis you?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: He was north of the cemetery --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. His function rather than his position.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: His function?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: He was my second in command. He was on a patrol and was checking the UNMOs at the cemetery -- wrong, at the stadium. And so he was north of the position looking south. He was my second in command and would have returned straight to PAPA headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did he make any suggestions that there was outgoing fire from the area of the Lion Cemetery which may have attracted incoming fire?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: No, nothing at all. If there had been, I'm sure he would have heard it. And if he had, I know he would have put it in the report and he would have told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have mentioned that the stadium was -- also received fire. Now, on the map we sort of see two circles -- ovals I guess they are called which resemble a stadium. By "stadium," which one are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: My stadium, the main olympic stadium which had the seating all the way around the outside, I can see the two. But this map isn't good enough for me to be able to remember which one it was going to be. It's the main olympic stadium. There's a football pitch in the middle of it. It has a running track. I could have made a mistake. It could be this one just here indicated on the map as the darker circle, which is largest as opposed to this one here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the darker circle which is largest, you referred to the circle which is in between number 4 and 5, but more to the left.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Between 4 and 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 4 and 3, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: There's 3. I was trying to see from the photographs to see exactly the distance between -- I'd need clarification or a better map to say if that is the main olympic stadium, and I may have to reconsider and say that yes, that is, because it has got all the seating, and so he would be where my pointer is now, which is on the eastern side of that stadium. And he could then see across to the Lion Cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the last question on this, and with your indulgence, Your Honours, I misjudged my time. I'm sure I'll get better. It's probably another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I noticed that as well. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi. And I would like to urge the parties to keep as strict as possible to the time limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was there fire into this stadium? Do you have any -- made any observations?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Underneath the stadium is where there were some weapons and the soldiers. The troops from PAPA 1 moved into the stadium, and their guns were under the stadium. Also under there were 120 millimetre mortars and the trucks that moved the artillery pieces. These were checked every day. There was an UNMO there, and they never moved. They were just down underneath under the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any agreement that they wouldn't be used in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: They were constantly monitored. I'm not aware of any agreement like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, two last points: The first one is, can you, again, tell us in relation to the PAPA UNMOs 1 to 4 when they were removed or moved to another location? Don't say where they were moved to, but just in your timely recollection when did that happen, if it happened. Perhaps UNMO PAPA 1 first.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: They were moved in September and October. And PAPA 6 would have been put in late October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And PAPA 2?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Again, September. It's difficult for me to identify the exact month. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: But it was realised that the UNMOs at PAPA 2 were not doing a proper observation job, and so another location was found for them. So that would have been, say, October 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about PAPA 3 and PAPA 4?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The personnel from PAPA 3 would have been withdrawn probably October. And again, judging from the photos I referred to earlier on, that would have been October 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the new PAPA 4, where was that position?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: PAPA 4 at the stadium, we had a new PAPA 6 that was put in place, and that would have been, again, October, November time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. If you could please refer to the map and mark the new PAPA 4, if you recall where that location was.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Well, we had a position within the stadium, PAPA 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it remained within the stadium?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes. That numbering. So the new positions were the PAPA 6 that was looking north, repositioned PAPA 2 looking south, and then the new PAPA 5 also looking south. If you were to draw the left and the right arcs of each observation post, they overlap.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you go to picture number 6 again, please. Are you able to see the confrontation line between the Bosnian Serb army and the ABiH, or at least some positions from the Bosnian Serbs? And can you please mark it on the photo.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness drew a V indicating that these are what?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: On picture number 6, I've drawn a V which is pointing to a building. That building overlooked the stadium. And when I first started, that's where sniper fire would come down, and you could -- into the stadium. And so that is approximately where the front line was when I first arrived. It was down the road from PAPA 3, passed the stadium, and then at the edge of the urban area which was just on the other side of the building marked with a V in picture number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so everything at the hill behind was -- were positions controlled by the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, all the high ground in the distance is Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just last -- one last question which may take one or two minutes. Were you aware, Mr. Harding, of a dead female that was found a couple of hundred metres away from the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was driving from the airport down the airport road towards the PTT. Because of the debris on the road, all the vehicles drive on the same side of the road. And then as we drove down, the driver pointed out that there was a dead person lying in the road. I was then told that that person was there all day, and was eventually moved by UN personnel with an armoured personnel carrier. I couldn't stop because I was in a soft-skinned vehicle in an area known to have a lot of snipers and small-arms fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I stop you there, Mr. Harding. Do you know it was in danger from which side of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: To stop there, you're in view of the Serbian forces on the front line there. It was a known area that was covered by Serb forces, Serb snipers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us on the map where that location was.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The witness just marked the location with a cross and the letters "CAS."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware in which part of the body the witness was shot at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We all know that time is running. We've all noticed that. But it would be a good idea if the Prosecution would pinpoint the time when all this was happening, because this has not been stated, neither by the Prosecution nor by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, could you please assist Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, do you recall the date this incident happened?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact date without looking through my diary, which I made at the time. But I was the subsector commander, and so it would have been between the 13th of November, 1992, and the 23rd of January, 1993, to give it a bracket. As for an exact date, I would need to look at the diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I repeat the question I just asked before my learned friend stood up: Are you aware which part of the body the woman was shot at?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Yes. Once I was informed that the body had been picked up. I went to the morgue at the Kosevo Hospital and saw the woman and inspected the body to see where she had been shot. She had been hit in the head either by a single shot from a high-velocity rifle or a piece of shrapnel because there was a very large exit hole. It was a single round that had killed her. I also asked to see what was with the body at the time, and there was a plastic bag with some sticks in it, firewood. It was definitely the body picked up from near the PTT as indicated on the map. It had a very distinct dark brown long coat. So to answer the question, in my professional opinion, it was a single shot from a sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was this woman?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: Between 21 and 25.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my last question, clarification again: In your statement you gave to an investigator, you said that this incident happened on the 29th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we object to the admission of this statement and therefore we cannot accept what was just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please explain why you -- do you want this part of the statement be read to the witness or -- I mean, what's your objection based on?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, the Prosecution is putting a leading question. The question follows from a document for which it has not yet been decided whether it will be admitted or not and that is why I am objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what the question was? As far as I can read in the transcript now, the question until you interrupted was: "Now, my last question, clarification again, in your statement you gave to an investigator you said that this incident happened on the 29th of January, 1993." I do not know what the question would be after. Or would you like the Prosecution first to establish whether this was part of the statement? I mean, if it's the Defence case that this is not part of the statement, then of course it would be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the problem is that the witness has just said very clearly, and this was before this question was put to him, that this event could only have taken place between two dates, one of which is a date that is before the 29th of January. The witness has, therefore, already specified a certain period, but in any case, it is up to you, Your Honours, to make a decision on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would be your question, Mr. Waespi? Because I do not know yet, since the statement you're confronting the witness with gives a different answer to what you earlier asked the witness -- to the earlier answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I started my issue with saying it's a clarification, because the witness had said this morning that he left I believe on the 23rd of January, and this is a week before this incident happened. So I wanted to ask him to clarify this issue. And the second point is, we don't intend to tender this witness statement. Of course not. It's just giving him a chance to clarify whether this heading of the incident, that female, 29th January, 1993, whether that's correct as he recalls today. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed. The objection is denied. The answer in view of the earlier statement clearly is in need of some clarification. We'll first hear what it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, can you tell us whether this incident which you talked about, indeed as you had stated in your witness statement, happened on the 29th of January, 1993, or on another date?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: To find out the exact date, I'd need to look in my diary. But it was definitely within my period there because I definitely remember searching the woman to see where the injuries were on her dead body. The reason I was saying the 23rd of January is that's when I thought I had finished my diary, but it was in my time as the subsector commander. So if there is a confusion in the dates, I would again have to look at the diary. But it was definitely within my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi. Is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. First, let Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. me thank you for giving us the floor. The last time we spent too much time, and you criticized us for good reason. Today, we have only about 10 minutes left, and I will not be here tomorrow, although I had told you earlier that I would be cross-examining this witness, we will have to make the best of it and change our plans. So I now wish to ask you to give us five minutes because I will not be here tomorrow. I can start this now, but I think the presence of the witness is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask my questions in French, one of the official languages of this Tribunal. Because we were unable to prepare for this cross-examination, I will ask you to give very short replies. My first question is: How many military corps were there in Sarajevo and which army did they belong to? For the interpreters, I'm speaking of the location.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The location Sarajevo, the 1st Corps of the Bosnian army, that was what I referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We all understand that we are speaking of Sarajevo, but precisely where in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The 1st Corps had elements deployed around, around the city, at various locations, which were then divided into individual units and commands. It all came under the 1st Corps headquarters, which I reported to on numerous occasions each week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, sir. Can you tell us now where exactly these headquarters were, the headquarters of the 1st Corps, the headquarters of the 1st battalion -- I apologise, of the 1st Brigade, the 2nd, and the 5th Motorised Brigade? Please, be very precise. In what streets? And if possible, give us the house number as well.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: The 1st Corps headquarters were a seven-minute walk north from PAPA headquarters. And they were in the basement of a multistorey building. Regarding other battalion headquarters, company headquarters, they were --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must interrupt you, sir. Please let us be short. I asked you whether you knew the name of the street and the house number. I will repeat my question: I asked you whether you knew the street and the house number. If you don't, tell us so.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: I was never informed of those because I knew where to walk to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if you don't know, you can just tell us you don't know. We would like to take up as little time as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, just two points a general one and a specific one. If my learned counsel could let the witness finish his answers, and we would like to offer that the witness be recalled at a later point so that the Defence also Mr. Piletta-Zanin can cross-examine the witness and has full time to do so. But I would really like that Mr. Harding is allowed to finish his answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree that if, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you ask a question, perhaps it's good first to listen to what the witness says, and if it's not precise enough. On the other hand, I do not mind to be quite honest that if the witness is giving descriptions that are more vague than Defence counsel would like to know. If, for example -- let's just take an example. If Mr. Piletta-Zanin just wants to know whether the witness is aware of the name of the street and the number of any headquarters, he is allowed to ask. I mean, it is a different question whether this Chamber might be interested to know even if he doesn't know the name of the street and the number of the building whether this Chamber might be interested to know where about the headquarters might have been. But I leave it to up to Mr. Piletta-Zanin to ask exactly what he wants to ask. But Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it might also be a bit a result of your question. You first tell us could you tell us where the headquarters were and your next question is, could you tell us very precise, and then you you'd like to know the name of the street and the number as well. If you just start asking are you aware of the names of the streets and the numbers of the buildings where the headquarters or the brigades, and then perhaps the 1st Brigade, then it goes far quicker, and you can come quite quicker to where you'd like to be as far as I understand you. So the more precise the question is the more precise you get the answer in a quick way. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the street number and the floor. We are still speaking of the 1st Corps, and I'm asking the precise address, the street, the house number, and the floor.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: No, I cannot tell you the street or the house number. It's on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And the 2nd Brigade, do you know the exact address, the street, the house number, and the floor?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the 2nd Brigade, the same question, the street, the house number, the floor?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the 5th Brigade, can you tell us the street, the house number, and the floor?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you whether you know at least something. Do you know this information for any brigade, any battalion? Could you tell us the precise address of any of these headquarters? If you can't, then tell us so.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this precise reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am now forced to put a question of a personal nature. This is my duty as Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this question is not meant to be an attack on you. I apologise for having to ask you it, but sir, I can see that today, you are disabled. I think you were not when you were in Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think we had clarified this point even before the witness came in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with you, that you clarified it. But I don't know. Did you inform the Defence on the details? Because the -- I can imagine that the Defence might not be willing to accept your -- good reasons to believe that your explanation might not be the right one, then of course -- I do not know, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is there any reason to doubt the explanation given by the Prosecution, that the handicap of Mr. Harding is not related in any way, as far as I understand, to the conflict in the former Yugoslavia? Is there any reason to have any doubt or is there any specific -- could you please tell us the relevance of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wished to be quite certain that there is absolutely no connection between the events we are referring to today and Mr. Harding's handicap. Of course, if there were any connection between these two events, it would have legal consequences. I know that this is a very personal question, but the reply to this question would clarify certain matters for all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever objection there may have been, I think it's -- the Defence is entitled to ask. And let me just look at your question precisely. Your first question -- your question was: "I think you were not when you were in Sarajevo. Is that correct?" So I think the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was my first question. I said I think that during your time in Sarajevo, you did not have this disability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But to avoid someone objecting to my putting such a personal question, I can leave it to the Trial Chamber to establish this and clarify the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since it may be experienced as a very sensible issue, I'll be glad to assist you. Mr. Harding, the Defence just wants to clarify whether there could be any relation between your handicap and your testimony in this Court. Your handicap, does it date from before your time in Sarajevo or from after your time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After the time in Sarajevo. Was it related in whatever way, I would say, to the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Nothing at all to do. I was involved in a road traffic accident in the United Kingdom in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think this clarifies the issue. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed. Thank you for giving this answer. I can understand it's a sensitive issue. You can understand why the Defence would like to make sure that there's no relation whatsoever. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I understand, you were involved in a road accident in 1997, and I am sorry about this. But this accident had no connection with, for example, a mission you may have been involved in in Great Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Britain that was connected to the previous events because as far as I know you were still serving in the military in great Britain after you returned from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think you clarified this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is my understanding, Mr. Harding, but please correct me if I am wrong, that this road accident had nothing to do in whatever way with either a mission related to the -- what I call the Balkans, just in very general terms. If I'm not correct in understanding, please tell me. If it's totally unrelated, Mr. Piletta-Zanin will put his next question to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time of my road traffic accident, I was an instructor at the Air Academy for the Royal Air Force. . It was instructional duties, and these instructional duties had nothing to do with the Balkans or anything outside of the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Apart from that, it is 4.00 now, I promised you five minutes which I did not give you yet. So I'd like to perhaps stop here if that's a convenient moment for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I think we agreed that the issues you'd like to raise do not necessarily have to be raised in the presence of the witness because they have not nothing to do with that. So therefore I would like to ask the usher to lead the witness out of the courtroom. Mr. Harding, we will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00, not at 9.30 as today but 9.00. Mr. Usher, could you...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for giving me the floor. There are two things I wish to say. As I told you before, I will be absent for reasons beyond my control. These are family matters. I have prepared as far as I was able to for a part of the cross-examination of this witness who, as we can see, cannot tell us where the headquarters of the various brigades were located. And I'm afraid that the witness will have to be recalled. The Defence has already said that they wished this witness to be recalled at some point. Tomorrow, my colleague will continue cross-examining the witness; however, there are some questions I would personally like to put to the witness in my own way, and I will be able to do this only later. This week, we shall be discussing the application of Rule 92 bis (e), and I would like to be present when this is done because I wish to expound certain aspects of this issue here. A trial in absentia would not be the correct thing to do in this case, so we wish to consider this issue not before Wednesday. I have tried to be brief and to put my points to you as briefly as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you first one clarification, if you say you'd like to have this witness recalled, do you mean Wednesday or Thursday, or do you mean on a longer term? I mean, how much time would you need to prepare for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you correctly see that the Defence also pays attention to the state of person.
